title: Ibrahim and the Hajj
intro: Eleven days through the first days of Dhul Hijjah: the story of the Prophet Ibrahim (Abraham) and the verses of the Hajj.

posts.display: By the Dawn And ten nights, And the Even and the Odd, And the night when it departeth.
posts.display_original: وَٱلْفَجْرِ وَلَيَالٍ عَشْرٍ وَٱلشَّفْعِ وَٱلْوَتْرِ وَٱلَّيْلِ إِذَا يَسْرِ
posts.caption: For many Muslims, Dhul Hijjah, the month of the Hajj pilgrimage, begins around now, depending on the moon. Many commentators, including Ibn Kathir, understood the "ten nights" of this oath as its first ten days, among the most honored of the year. Over the coming days: the Prophet Ibrahim (Abraham), whose story the Hajj retraces.

Al-An'am tells how Ibrahim watched a star, the moon and then the sun rise and set, and concluded that none of them could be his Lord. These are his words as he turns to the Creator. Pickthall's "by nature upright" translates hanif, a word the Quran often uses for Ibrahim.

posts.display: And (remember) when his Lord tried Abraham with (His) commands, and he fulfilled them, He said: Lo! I have appointed thee a leader for mankind.
posts.display_original: وَإِذِ ٱبْتَلَىٰٓ إِبْرَٰهِـۧمَ رَبُّهُۥ بِكَلِمَٰتٍ فَأَتَمَّهُنَّ قَالَ إِنِّى جَاعِلُكَ لِلنَّاسِ إِمَامًا
posts.caption: In Al-Baqarah, Ibrahim is tested with "commands", fulfils them, and is made an imam, a leader, for humankind. Ibn Kathir records several views of what the commands were, including the rites of Hajj and the great trials of his life: being thrown into a fire by his people, leaving his homeland, and the command to sacrifice his son.

In As-Saffat, Ibrahim leaves his homeland: "I am going unto my Lord". He prays for a righteous child and is given good news of "a gentle son", ghulam halim. Most Muslim commentators identify this son as Ismail (Ishmael), whose story runs through the days of Hajj.

posts.display: Our Lord! Lo! I have settled some of my posterity in an uncultivable valley near unto Thy holy House, our Lord! that they may establish proper worship.
posts.display_original: رَّبَّنَآ إِنِّىٓ أَسْكَنتُ مِن ذُرِّيَّتِى بِوَادٍ غَيْرِ ذِى زَرْعٍ عِندَ بَيْتِكَ ٱلْمُحَرَّمِ رَبَّنَا لِيُقِيمُوا۟ ٱلصَّلَوٰةَ
posts.caption: Muslim tradition tells that Ibrahim left his wife Hajar (Hagar) and their baby Ismail in the dry valley of Mecca, trusting Allah. Hajar's search for water between the hills of Safa and Marwa, and the spring of Zamzam that followed, are remembered in the rites of Hajj. This is part of Ibrahim's prayer for them.

Ibrahim and his son Ismail raise the foundations of the Kaaba, the House in Mecca that Muslims face in prayer. Their words are not about the work itself but a request: accept it from us. Muslims often say this short prayer, rabbana taqabbal minna, after finishing a good deed.

posts.display: And proclaim unto mankind the pilgrimage. They will come unto thee on foot and on every lean camel; they will come from every deep ravine.
posts.caption: In Al-Hajj, Ibrahim is told to proclaim the pilgrimage to all people, with the promise that they will come from "every deep ravine". Pilgrims arriving in Mecca in these days call out the talbiyah, "Here I am, O Allah, here I am", often understood as an answer to that call.

posts.display: (Abraham) said: O my dear son, I have seen in a dream that I must sacrifice thee. So look, what thinkest thou? He said: O my father! Do that which thou art commanded. Allah willing, thou shalt find me of the steadfast.
posts.display_original: قَالَ يَٰبُنَىَّ إِنِّىٓ أَرَىٰ فِى ٱلْمَنَامِ أَنِّىٓ أَذْبَحُكَ فَٱنظُرْ مَاذَا تَرَىٰ قَالَ يَٰٓأَبَتِ ٱفْعَلْ مَا تُؤْمَرُ سَتَجِدُنِىٓ إِن شَآءَ ٱللَّهُ مِنَ ٱلصَّٰبِرِينَ
posts.caption: Ibrahim tells his son of a dream that he must sacrifice him, and asks his view. The son's calm answer is one of the most moving lines in the Quran, and Allah ransoms him a few verses later. Around now, on the eighth of Dhul Hijjah, pilgrims move to Mina, where this story is remembered.

posts.display: This day have I perfected your religion for you and completed My favour unto you, and have chosen for you as religion al-Islam.
posts.display_original: ٱلْيَوْمَ أَكْمَلْتُ لَكُمْ دِينَكُمْ وَأَتْمَمْتُ عَلَيْكُمْ نِعْمَتِى وَرَضِيتُ لَكُمُ ٱلْإِسْلَٰمَ دِينًا
posts.caption: For many Muslims the Day of Arafah falls around now: pilgrims stand in prayer on the plain of Arafat, and many elsewhere fast. Many Sunni commentators, following a report from Umar, date this verse to Arafah during the Farewell Pilgrimage of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ in 632 CE; Shia tradition links it with Ghadir Khumm days later.

posts.display: Their flesh and their food reach not Allah, but the devotion from you reacheth Him.
posts.display_original: لَن يَنَالَ ٱللَّهَ لُحُومُهَا وَلَا دِمَآؤُهَا وَلَٰكِن يَنَالُهُ ٱلتَّقْوَىٰ مِنكُمْ
posts.caption: Eid al-Adha, the Festival of Sacrifice, falls around now: on this Sunday for many Muslims, on Monday for others. Those who can afford it sacrifice an animal and share the meat with family, neighbors and the poor, remembering Ibrahim. This verse says what reaches Allah is not the meat but the devotion, taqwa, behind it. Eid Mubarak.

posts.display_original: إِنَّآ أَعْطَيْنَٰكَ ٱلْكَوْثَرَ فَصَلِّ لِرَبِّكَ وَٱنْحَرْ إِنَّ شَانِئَكَ هُوَ ٱلْأَبْتَرُ
posts.caption: Al-Kawthar is the Quran's shortest surah. "Abundance" translates al-kawthar, which many commentators describe as a river or pool in Paradise given to the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ. Its call to "pray and sacrifice" echoes these days of Eid, still being celebrated around now. Eid Mubarak, and thank you for following the story of Ibrahim.
